title: K-th Fastest Finisher
aka: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
story: At a city marathon, each finishing time in seconds goes into a binary search tree as the runner crosses the line: faster left, slower right. The tree is never re-sorted, so its shape depends on finishing order.
The prize table calls runners by place: the 3rd fastest, the 10th for a spot prize. The tree already keeps times in order, so there is no need to copy them out and sort.
task: Write kthFastest(root, k). root is a valid binary search tree. Return its k-th smallest value (k = 1 is the smallest).

All times are different, and k is between 1 and the number of nodes. Trees are shown in level order, like [9000, 8000, 9500], with null for a missing child. Your function receives real TreeNode objects with val, left and right.
constraints: The tree is a valid binary search tree, at most 500 levels deep.

examples.explanation: In sorted order the times are 7800, 8000, 8600, 9000, 9200, 9500 and 9900, so the 3rd is 8600. The 3rd value in the tree layout is 9500, and that is the wrong answer.
Place 7 of 7 is the slowest runner, which is the rightmost node. Places count from 1, so k = 7 is the last runner and not past the end.

hints: In a search tree, where is the fastest time? Which time comes right after it?
Left subtree, then node, then right subtree visits the values from smallest to largest. That order is called in-order.
So the answer is the k-th node an in-order walk visits. Do you need to finish the walk once you reach k?
Do an in-order walk with a counter (recursively, or with a stack: push nodes while going left, pop one, count it, then go to its right child). When the counter reaches k, return that value and stop.
bruteForce: Collect every time into a list, sort it, and return the item at k - 1. That is O(n log n) and always visits all n runners, even when you only want the fastest.
The sort is wasted work, because the tree already stores the times in order. An in-order walk reads them in sorted order and can stop after k of them.

walkthrough: In a binary search tree, left is smaller and right is larger, so "left subtree, node, right subtree" visits values in sorted order. Count as you visit and stop at k.
1. Start at 9000 and keep going left, pushing 9000, 8000 and 7800 onto the stack.
• Pop 7800. The count is 1, and it has no right child.
• Pop 8000. The count is 2. Go right to 8600 and keep going left, which pushes only 8600.
• Pop 8600. The count is 3, which equals k, so return 8600.
9500, 9200 and 9900 are never touched. The explicit stack does the job of the recursion, and it makes stopping at k easy.
solution.timeWhy: You slide down at most h nodes to reach the smallest, then visit k nodes in order (each slide is paid for once).
solution.spaceWhy: The stack holds at most one path from the root, so at most h nodes.
solution.takeaway: An in-order walk of a binary search tree yields its values in sorted order. When a search-tree question mentions rank, order, "next larger" or "k-th", use in-order traversal and stop once you have enough.
